blogs.title: Standing, Speculation, and FOIA: The D.C. Circuit Closes the Door on Suits to Force OSC Investigations
blogs.description: The panel held that America First Legal lacked Article III standing to compel the Office of Special Counsel to investigate alleged FOIA misconduct at DOJ. The opinion tightens both causation and redressability: injuries from withheld DOJ records are traceable to DOJ, not OSC, and the supposed causal chain—OSC investigation to MSPB sanctions to DOJ compliance—rests on independent actors and enforcement discretion. The court also rejected informational-standing theories because § 1216 confers no entitlement to receive information from OSC and any § 1214 investigative notices are discretionary in § 1216 matters. Relying on Summers, Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine, Haaland v. Brackeen, and recent D.C. Circuit precedent like Hecate Energy, the decision underscores that relaxed procedural-injury doctrine still demands a concrete injury and non-speculative redressability. The result fortifies a boundary: FOIA’s informational injury gets you into court against the withholding agency, not against a separate enforcement body.

blogs.title: Who Polices FOIA Misconduct? The Unresolved Tension Between § 1216 and FOIA § 552(a)(4)(F)
blogs.description: The district court had read 5 U.S.C. § 1216’s command that OSC “shall…conduct an investigation” of arbitrary FOIA withholdings as independent of FOIA’s referral trigger in § 552(a)(4)(F); the D.C. Circuit vacated on standing and left that merits question open. This post explores the statutory architecture: Congress created a bespoke FOIA discipline mechanism that requires a court order, a fee award, and a specific judicial finding before OSC must initiate proceedings, while § 1216 broadly authorizes OSC to investigate non-PPP misconduct and to proceed under §§ 1214 and 1215. Carson v. OSC suggests OSC retains discretion over importing § 1214 procedures into § 1216 inquiries, complicating any claim of a justiciable, mandatory duty. The unresolved interplay matters for agency design and incentives: if § 1216 truly mandates investigations outside § 552(a)(4)(F), OSC’s docket and MSPB’s role could expand; if not, FOIA discipline remains largely channeled through the rare § 552(a)(4)(F) referral. The court’s jurisdictional disposition preserves uncertainty and invites either congressional clarification or a future case with a plaintiff who can establish standing.

blogs.title: Chaney’s Long Shadow: Why Private Plaintiffs Can’t Conscript Executive Enforcement
blogs.description: Although framed as a standing case, the opinion leans on Heckler v. Chaney to illustrate why courts will not police the Executive’s investigative and disciplinary choices. The redressability analysis treats OSC’s enforcement decisions, the MSPB’s potential sanctions, and DOJ’s production choices as independent judgments beyond a court’s control, reinforcing Chaney’s nonreviewability baseline. Norton v. SUWA’s promise of compelling discrete, legally required action offers little help where an asserted “shall investigate” duty does not confer a concrete, plaintiff-centered entitlement and remedial steps remain discretionary. The decision signals a broader separation-of-powers throughline in recent standing cases: plaintiffs cannot leverage generalized oversight provisions to obtain judicial control over how executive-branch watchdogs set priorities. Expect this reasoning to spill over to efforts to compel Inspectors General, ethics offices, and similar bodies to investigate.

blogs.title: After AFL v. Greer: A Practitioner’s Playbook for Prompting OSC FOIA Discipline the Right Way
blogs.description: For litigants hoping to spur OSC to act on FOIA abuses, this case is a roadmap of what not to do. Suing OSC directly stumbles on standing and redressability because FOIA’s informational injury runs against the withholding agency, and § 1216 creates no right to receive investigation updates. The viable path remains the FOIA suit itself: build a record, seek a court order compelling production, obtain a fee award, and press for a specific judicial finding questioning whether the withholding was arbitrary or capricious—only then does § 552(a)(4)(F) require OSC to initiate proceedings. Where the grievance is a systemic practice (like a refusal to search emails), pursue a Payne-style policy-or-practice claim within FOIA to secure injunctive relief. The lesson is strategic rather than jurisdictional: use FOIA to fix FOIA, and let § 552(a)(4)(F) operate as the back-end discipline trigger rather than trying to conscript OSC on the front end.
